unit-alg-0105.title: Topic 1 · 1-5 Solving Equations and Inequalities by Graphing
unit-alg-0105.srcName: enVision Algebra 2, Lesson 1-5 Solving Equations and Inequalities by Graphing (Drive)

summary.text: Using graphs and tables to solve equations and inequalities: graph each side as its own function, read the x-values where they cross, and for an inequality read where the graph sits above or below zero. Also covers refining an estimate with a table and with graphing technology.

why.text: This is where equations stop being pure symbol-pushing. A graph tells you how many solutions there are and roughly where before you do any algebra — and for equations that mix an absolute value with a line, or a parabola with a line, the picture is what stops you from finding one solution and missing the other.

objectives.text: Solve a linear, absolute-value or quadratic equation by graphing each side and reading the crossings.
Solve a one-variable inequality by graphing and reading where the function is above or below zero.
Refine an estimated solution using a table of values or graphing technology.
Model a head-start or catch-up situation as an inequality and interpret the solution.
Say why a system produced no solution, using both the algebra and the picture.

parentNote.text: Built from the enVision Lesson 1-5 textbook pages. The questions are fresh rather than copies of the practice sheets, so the sheets stay usable as homework. Two things trip most students here: reading the answer as the whole intersection point instead of the x-value, and on inequalities like x² − 4 > 0, looking for where x is positive rather than where the expression is. Both have their own card and their own question. Three questions carry graphs.

nextUp.text: Start with the flashcards, especially the two about the common traps, then take the quiz. The graph questions are the ones worth slowing down on.

cards.def:
**Graph each side as its own function and read the x-values where they cross.**
• y = left side, y = right side.
• Every intersection gives one solution.
• The solution is the x-value, not the whole point.
cards.hint: Two expressions are equal exactly where their graphs meet.

cards.term: Why the x-value, not the point
cards.def:
**The point (5, 5) means x = 5 is the solution — the y-value is just what both sides equal there.**
• Writing (5, 5) as the answer answers a different question.
• Check by substituting the x back into the original equation.
cards.hint: The question asked what x is. The y is a by-product.

cards.def:
**Move everything to one side, graph that function, and read where the graph is above or below zero.**
• For f(x) > 0, find where the curve is above the x-axis.
• The x-intercepts are where the answer switches.
cards.hint: The x-axis is the zero line. Above it is positive.

cards.def:
**You are looking for where y is greater than 0, not where x is.**
• The intercepts are x = −2 and x = 2.
• The curve is above the axis outside them: x < −2 or x > 2.
cards.hint: Read the height of the graph, not the position along the axis.

cards.def:
**Where one graph sits above the other, that expression is the larger one.**
• Their intersection is the switch-over point.
• Below the crossing, the other one leads.
cards.hint: Higher on the page means bigger in value.

cards.def:
**The head start is a constant added to the slower traveller's distance, not to the faster one's.**
• Car at 60 mph vs motorcycle at 40 mph with a 40-mile lead: 60x > 40x + 40.
• The crossing is when the chaser draws level.
cards.hint: Whoever started ahead carries the extra distance in their expression.

cards.def:
**Parallel lines never meet, so the equation has no solution.**
• Solving 3x − 5 = 2 + 3x algebraically gives −5 = 2, which is false.
• Equal slopes and different intercepts is the graphical version of that contradiction.
cards.hint: A false statement with no x left in it means no solution.

cards.def:
**A round bracket excludes the endpoint; a square bracket includes it.**
• x > 2 is (2, ∞).
• x ≥ 2 is [2, ∞).
• Infinity always takes a round bracket, because you never reach it.
cards.hint: Strict inequality, round bracket. Or-equal-to, square bracket.

cards.def:
**When the crossing is not at a neat value, tabulate both sides and find where the difference is smallest.**
• Narrow the interval a decimal place at a time.
• The x whose two outputs are closest is the best estimate so far.
cards.hint: Squeeze the interval until the two columns nearly agree.

cards.def:
**Graphing technology reports the crossing to several decimals, but you still choose the rounding the question asks for.**
• Enter each side as its own function.
• A curve can cross a line twice — check for a second intersection.
cards.hint: The calculator finds one crossing at a time. Look for others.

cards.def:
**A V-shaped graph usually meets a line twice, so expect two solutions.**
• |x − 4| = ½x + 1 crosses at x = 2 and x = 10.
• Finding only one usually means the other branch was missed.
cards.hint: A V has two arms. Check both.

cards.def:
**Substitute the x back into the ORIGINAL equation and confirm both sides land on the same number.**
• A graph read by eye is an estimate until it is checked.
• This catches a misread scale immediately.
cards.hint: The graph suggests. The substitution confirms.

cards.def:
**If a graph crosses between two grid lines, the solution is between those two x-values.**
• The signs of the difference flip across the crossing.
• That bracket is the starting point for a table.
cards.hint: A sign change between two x-values traps a solution between them.

cards.def:
**Graphing shows how many solutions there are and roughly where, even when the algebra is hard or impossible.**
• It also shows at a glance whether a system has none, one, or many.
• Algebra then gives the exact values.
cards.hint: The graph tells you what to expect. The algebra pins it down.

questions.q: To solve 2x + 1 = x + 5 by graphing, which two functions should you graph?
questions.hint: Set y equal to each side of the equation separately.
steps: Graphing solves an equation by comparing the two sides as separate functions.
Let y equal the left side: y = 2x + 1. Let y equal the right side: y = x + 5.
Where those two graphs cross, the two sides are equal, and that x is the solution.

ex.main: **y = 2x + 1 and y = x + 5.** Two sides, two functions, and the crossing is where they agree.
ex.tip: Combining the sides first is the algebraic method, not the graphical one.

questions.q: The graphs of y = −3x + 20 and y = 0.2x + 4 shown cross at (5, 5). What is the solution of −3x + 20 = 0.2x + 4?
questions.hint: The question asks for x. The y-value is what both sides equal there.
steps: The crossing point is (5, 5).
The solution of an equation in one variable is an x-value, so read the x-coordinate.
x = 5. Check: −3(5) + 20 = 5 and 0.2(5) + 4 = 5, so both sides agree.

ex.main: **x = 5.** The 5 in the y-position is simply the value both sides take there.
ex.tip: Solving for one variable means the answer is one number, not a point.

questions.q: The graph of y = x² − 4 shown crosses the x-axis at −2 and 2. Over which interval is x² − 4 greater than 0?
questions.hint: Greater than 0 means the curve is ABOVE the x-axis.
steps: x² − 4 > 0 asks where the height of the graph is above zero.
The curve dips below the axis between its intercepts and rises above outside them.
So x² − 4 > 0 when x < −2 or x > 2.

ex.main: **x < −2 or x > 2.** The common slip is answering x > 0 — but the question is about the value of the expression, not the sign of x.
ex.tip: Ask "is the graph above or below the axis here", never "is x positive here".

questions.q: Solve −x + 4 = 2 by graphing.
questions.hint: Where does the line y = −x + 4 reach a height of 2?
steps: Graph y = −x + 4 and the horizontal line y = 2.
They meet where −x + 4 = 2, that is where x = 2.

ex.main: **x = 2.** A constant on one side is a horizontal line, which makes the crossing easy to read.
ex.tip: An equation with a number on one side is always a horizontal-line problem.

questions.q: Which interval notation means x ≥ 3?
questions.hint: Or-equal-to includes the endpoint. Infinity never gets a square bracket.
steps: x ≥ 3 includes 3 itself, so the 3 takes a square bracket.
The values run upward without end, so the right end is ∞ with a round bracket.

ex.main: **[3, ∞).** Square bracket includes the endpoint; infinity is never included because it is not a number you reach.
ex.tip: A bracket next to ∞ is always round.

questions.q: The graphs of y = |x − 4| and y = ½x + 1 shown cross at (2, 2) and (10, 6). What are the solutions of |x − 4| = ½x + 1?
questions.hint: A V-shaped graph usually meets a line on both arms.
steps: The two graphs cross twice, at (2, 2) and at (10, 6).
Each crossing gives one solution, read from the x-coordinate.

ex.main: **x = 2 and x = 10.** Stopping at the first crossing is the usual way to lose half the answer.
ex.tip: Count the crossings before you write anything down.

questions.q: Solving 3x − 5 = 2 + 3x algebraically gives −5 = 2. What does the graph look like?
opts: Two parallel lines that never meet
questions.hint: What kind of statement is −5 = 2?
steps: Subtracting 3x from both sides leaves −5 = 2, which is false for every x.
A false statement with no variable left means no value of x works.
Graphically, both sides have slope 3 but different intercepts: parallel lines that never meet.

ex.main: **Two parallel lines that never meet.** Equal slopes with different intercepts is the picture of "no solution".
ex.tip: If the variable vanishes and the leftover statement is false, there is no solution.

questions.q: Solve −¼x + 6 = ½x + 3 by graphing.
questions.hint: Set the two sides equal and gather the x terms.
steps: Graph y = −¼x + 6 and y = ½x + 3 and look for the crossing.
Algebraically: 6 − 3 = ½x + ¼x, so 3 = ¾x.

ex.main: **x = 4.** Both sides land on 5 there, which is exactly what the crossing point shows.
ex.tip: Confirm a graphical read with one substitution — it costs seconds.

questions.q: Solve ¾x = 2x − 10 by graphing.
questions.hint: Where is the steeper line finally as high as the shallower one?
steps: Graph y = ¾x and y = 2x − 10.
Algebraically: 10 = 2x − ¾x = 1¼x, so x = 10 ÷ 1.25.

ex.main: **x = 8.** Both sides equal 6 at that x, so the lines cross at (8, 6).
ex.tip: A fractional coefficient is easier to handle as a decimal when checking.

questions.q: Solve the inequality x² + x − 6 < 0 by graphing.
questions.hint: Less than 0 means the curve is BELOW the x-axis.
steps: Factor to find where the graph meets the axis: x² + x − 6 = (x + 3)(x − 2), so the intercepts are −3 and 2.
An upward parabola dips below the axis between its intercepts.
So x² + x − 6 < 0 when −3 < x < 2.

ex.main: **−3 < x < 2.** Upward parabola, below the axis, means the inside interval.
ex.tip: Upward parabola: negative between the roots, positive outside them.

questions.q: Solve x − 5 > −2x + 4 by graphing.
questions.hint: Where does the rising line sit above the falling one?
steps: Graph y = x − 5 and y = −2x + 4; they cross where x − 5 = −2x + 4.
3x = 9, so the crossing is at x = 3.
To the right of the crossing the rising line is on top, so x > 3.

ex.main: **x > 3.** Find the crossing first, then decide which side of it the inequality describes.
ex.tip: After finding the crossing, test one convenient x to pick the correct side.

questions.q: A car travelling 60 mph is 40 miles behind a motorcycle travelling 40 mph. Which inequality says the car is ahead?
questions.hint: The head start belongs to whoever started in front.
steps: Let x be the hours since the car set off. The car covers 60x miles.
The motorcycle started 40 miles ahead, so its distance from the car's start is 40x + 40.
The car is ahead when 60x > 40x + 40, which solves to x > 2.

ex.main: **60x > 40x + 40.** Adding the head start to the car is the classic slip — it belongs to the vehicle that was already in front.
ex.tip: Write both distances from the same starting line before comparing them.

questions.q: Cindy is longboarding 6 miles ahead of Tamira at 2 mph. Tamira travels at 4 mph. After how long is Tamira ahead?
questions.hint: Set Tamira's distance above Cindy's, remembering the 6-mile lead.
steps: Let x be hours since Tamira started. Tamira covers 4x; Cindy is at 2x + 6.
Tamira leads when 4x > 2x + 6, so 2x > 6.
x > 3 — Tamira is ahead after 3 hours.

ex.main: **After 3 hours.** At exactly 3 hours they are level at 12 miles, and past that Tamira leads.
ex.tip: The gap closes at the difference of the speeds: 6 miles at 2 mph of closing is 3 hours.

questions.q: A graph of f(x) shows f(0.6) = −1.04 and f(0.7) = −1.31, while g(0.6) = −1.4 and g(0.7) = −1.3. Between which values does f(x) = g(x)?
questions.hint: Look at which function is on top at each end.
steps: At x = 0.6, f is −1.04 and g is −1.4, so f is above g.
At x = 0.7, f is −1.31 and g is −1.3, so g is now above f.
They swapped places, so the graphs crossed somewhere between 0.6 and 0.7.

ex.main: **Between 0.6 and 0.7.** A swap in which function is larger guarantees a crossing in between.
ex.tip: Tables find crossings by watching for the moment the ordering flips.

questions.q: Ben says the solution of −x² + 9 > 0 is x < −3 or x > 3. What went wrong?
opts: The parabola opens downward, so it is above the axis BETWEEN −3 and 3
The intercepts are at −9 and 9, not −3 and 3
questions.hint: Which way up does y = −x² + 9 open?
steps: The intercepts are where −x² + 9 = 0, so x = ±3. Ben got those right.
The leading coefficient is negative, so the parabola opens DOWNWARD.
A downward parabola is above the axis between its intercepts, so the answer is −3 < x < 3. Ben gave the outside interval, which belongs to an upward parabola.

ex.main: **The parabola opens downward, so the solution is −3 < x < 3.** Ben applied the upward-parabola pattern without checking the sign in front of x².
ex.tip: Check the direction the curve opens before deciding inside or outside.

questions.q: Solve −x² − 2x + 15 ≤ 0.
questions.hint: Multiplying by −1 flips the inequality sign.
steps: Multiply through by −1 and flip the sign: x² + 2x − 15 ≥ 0.
Factor: (x + 5)(x − 3) ≥ 0, so the intercepts are −5 and 3.
An upward parabola is at or above zero outside its roots: x ≤ −5 or x ≥ 3.

ex.main: **x ≤ −5 or x ≥ 3.** Forgetting to flip the sign when multiplying by a negative turns the answer inside out.
ex.tip: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative always reverses it.

questions.q: A graph shows the solution of −½x + 7/2 = −x + a is x = −1. What is a?
questions.hint: Substitute x = −1 into both sides and solve for a.
steps: If x = −1 is the solution, both sides are equal there.
Right side: −(−1) + a = 1 + a. Setting 1 + a = 4 gives a = 3.

ex.main: **a = 3.** When the solution is given, the unknown constant is found by substituting rather than by graphing.
ex.tip: A known solution turns a graphing problem into a one-line substitution.

questions.q: Solve x² − 3 = x + 3 by graphing.
questions.hint: Bring everything to one side and factor.
steps: Graph y = x² − 3 and y = x + 3 and look for the crossings.
Algebraically: x² − x − 6 = 0, which factors to (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0.

ex.main: **x = −2 and x = 3.** A parabola and a line usually cross twice, so two solutions is the expected shape of the answer.
ex.tip: The sign of each root is worth checking — swapping them is easy and costly.

questions.q: Jack is running 2.45 miles ahead of Zhang. Jack runs 5.5 mph, Zhang 7.75 mph. When is Zhang ahead, to the nearest hundredth of an hour?
questions.hint: Zhang leads when 7.75x > 5.5x + 2.45.
steps: Let x be hours since Zhang started. Zhang covers 7.75x; Jack is at 5.5x + 2.45.
Zhang leads when 7.75x > 5.5x + 2.45, so 2.25x > 2.45.
x > 2.45 ÷ 2.25 = 1.0888…, which rounds to 1.09 hours.

ex.main: **After about 1.09 hours.** The closing speed is the difference, 2.25 mph, and it must eat a 2.45-mile lead.
ex.tip: Head-start problems always reduce to gap divided by closing speed.

questions.q: Why can graphing solve an equation that is difficult to solve algebraically?
opts: It gives exact answers no algebra can reach
It shows how many solutions exist and roughly where, so they can then be refined
It converts every equation into a linear one
It only works when the solutions are whole numbers
questions.hint: What does a picture tell you that a rearrangement does not?
steps: A graph shows every place the two sides meet, so it reveals the NUMBER of solutions at a glance.
It also shows roughly where each one sits, which gives a starting interval.
Tables or technology then refine those estimates to whatever precision is asked for.

ex.main: **It shows how many solutions exist and roughly where.** Graphing is a locating tool; the precision comes afterwards from tables or technology.
ex.tip: Graph to find out what to look for, then refine.
